title: Restoration economy

definition.text: The restoration economy is the economic activity that comes from repairing land and nature, such as ecological restoration work.

facts.text: It is set against economic activity built on sprawl or on extracting and using up natural resources.
The idea is that repairing past damage to nature and communities often pays off economically at local, regional and national scales.
The phrase became popular after Storm Cunningham's 2002 book The Restoration Economy, which sorted restorative development into eight sectors.
Four of the sectors focus on nature: ecological restoration, watershed restoration, fishery restoration and regenerative agriculture.
Restoration projects need workers, materials and services, so spending on them can create jobs and business activity in local economies.
A study across Oregon found 15-24 jobs per million invested, and each dollar generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars of economic activity.
The same Oregon study found restoration spending has similar economic and job effects to public infrastructure such as road building.
Hand work such as tree planting and thinning tends to pay less than logging, is less reliable, and is mostly done by immigrant workers.

notes: Namibia bush-biomass and South Africa ARISE examples (S:f2743ae6fe46, S:925755953885) usable as illustrations.

title: Afforestation

definition.text: Afforestation is creating a forest or stand of trees on land that has had no recent tree cover.

facts.text: It differs from reforestation, which turns back into forest land that once held forest but was converted to another use.
There are three types: natural regeneration, agroforestry and tree plantations.
It can help slow climate change by storing carbon in trees.
New trees can raise local rainfall, block strong winds, and reduce soil erosion, floods and landslides.
Projects create jobs, especially in rural areas, and supply wood products.
The process starts by choosing a site and studying its climate, soil, vegetation and human use, which decide the tree species and planting method.
Researchers debate whether it is always beneficial, since tree planting is not the only way to capture carbon.
Australia, Canada, China, India, Israel, the United States and Europe run afforestation programs, some also to reduce desertification.

contested_note: Researchers debate whether afforestation always helps, especially where land was never forest.

title: Afforestation of grasslands and savannas

definition.text: A criticism of tree-planting campaigns that put forests where they would not grow naturally, such as grasslands and savannas.

facts.text: Critics say treeless ecosystems are not necessarily degraded and can store carbon already; savannas and tundra store it underground.
Grasslands and savannas need their own management, since they are not meant to be forests.
Carbon forecasts for such programs often leave out soil carbon losses and the slowing of tree growth over time.

contested_note: Whether planting trees on naturally open land helps or harms is debated.

definition.text: New forest canopy can darken Earth's surface, lowering its albedo so it absorbs more heat and may warm the planet.

facts.text: The effect matters most in snowy regions, where white snow reflects far more sunlight than dark forest.
The extra heat absorbed by trees could cancel part of the carbon benefit of afforestation.
A 2023 study using 176 flux stations found a trade-off: more carbon uptake from afforestation comes with lower albedo.
Tropical reforestation instead helps form clouds that reflect sunlight and lower temperatures.

definition.text: A criticism of planting forests of a single tree species, often conifers: tree cover rises but the varied habitat wildlife needs is missing.

facts.text: Single-species plantations are often planted for commerce or easy management and lack the biodiversity of natural forests.
They offer limited food, shelter and nesting sites, and dense conifers let little light reach the forest floor.
A meta-analysis found mixed-species plantations would store more carbon alongside other benefits.

definition.text: Reforestation is restoring forests and woodlands that once stood on a site but were destroyed or damaged.

facts.text: The earlier loss may have come from deforestation, clearcutting or wildfire.
Programs have three main purposes: growing wood to harvest, slowing climate change, and restoring ecosystems and habitat.
It differs from afforestation, which makes new forest on land that was not forest before.
Reforestation and cutting deforestation store more carbon by enlarging forests, making them denser in carbon, replacing fossil fuels with forest products, and avoiding emissions from forest loss.
Because new trees take decades to match mature tropical forests, reducing deforestation usually helps the climate more than reforestation.
Up to 90% of newly planted seedlings often fail.
Some reforestation trees, such as Eucalyptus globulus, draw so much water from the soil that other plants cannot grow.
Large programs, such as China's Three-North 'Great Green Wall' begun in 1978, blur the line between reforestation and afforestation.

definition.text: Plantation forests are intensively managed stands of one or two tree species of the same age, planted in regular rows mainly to produce wood.

facts.text: They cover about 131 million ha: 3% of the world's forest area and 45% of all planted forest.
Planted forests grew from 4.1% to 7.0% of total forest area between 1990 and 2015.
Other planted forests, 55 percent of the total, are not intensively managed and may come to resemble natural forests; they can serve restoration and soil and water protection.
Over 90% of the world's forests regrow naturally rather than by planting.
Of planted forests worldwide, 18% of the area holds exotic species and the rest native ones.
Plantations are often monocultures, which brings drawbacks such as biodiversity loss.

conflicts.text: Plantation forests made up 280 million ha in 2015.
conflicts.note: The lead gives 280 million ha for plantation forests in 2015, while the methods section gives about 131 million ha; the 280 million ha figure may refer to all planted forests.

definition.text: Payments, credits and tax breaks that reward landowners or countries for replanting forests or for not cutting them down.

facts.text: A proposed 'compensated reduction' scheme would pay developing countries that cut emissions from deforestation over an agreed period.
Under that proposal the scheme is voluntary, but a country that signs up must cut emissions, and a missed target rolls into its next period.
Selling carbon sequestration credits to companies and people offsetting their footprint is an emerging way to fund reforestation.
Carbon credits let farmers and private landowners earn money from replanting while gaining healthier soil.
Governments also offer tax breaks to encourage companies to support reforestation.

title: Land competition in reforestation
article: Reforestation#Competition with other land uses and displacement risk

definition.text: The problem that reforestation can take land and water needed for food, grazing and housing, and may push out people who use that land.

facts.text: Government reforestation pledges add up to 1.2bn hectares by 2060, a tenth of the world's land area, which is seen as unrealistic.
Almost 300 million people live on land in the Global South identified as tropical forest restoration opportunity.
Agroforestry, such as growing coffee under trees, can blend forests with other land uses.
Programs focused on carbon storage rather than nearby communities' needs have been criticised.

contested_note: A WRI and IUCN map of 2 billion hectares for forest restoration is criticised for including 900 million hectares of grassland.

definition.text: The risk that carbon stored by reforestation returns to the air, for example through fire, insect outbreaks or harvesting.

facts.text: Harvesting and using wood from reforested land limits how long its carbon stays stored.
Nearly half of the Bonn Challenge pledges were found to be areas set aside for commercial wood use.
Emissions from damage to tropical rainforests may be underestimated by a factor of six.
Many standards hold buffer reserves of credits and keep monitoring to manage such reversals.

definition.text: Ecological restoration is helping an ecosystem recover after it has been degraded, damaged, destroyed or transformed.

facts.text: It differs from conservation by repairing ecosystems already damaged rather than preventing damage.
It can help reverse biodiversity loss, fight climate change, keep ecosystem services flowing and support local economies.
Methods include erosion control, reforestation, weed and non-native species removal, reintroducing native species and building wildlife corridors.
Restoration ecology is the scientific study of restoration; ecological restoration is the practical work.
Projects have grown exponentially, with hundreds of thousands worldwide.
Reasons include restoring natural capital such as clean water, helping endangered species, adapting to climate change and storing carbon.
Restorations often miss their goals, and high costs can be seen as a drawback; public support fades if costs seem to outweigh benefits.
The United Nations named 2021–2030 the Decade on Ecosystem Restoration.

title: Restoration targets and baselines

definition.text: The choice of what state a restored ecosystem should aim for, traditionally a past 'historic baseline' thought to be pristine.

facts.text: Human-driven change, including climate change, keeps altering ecosystems, producing a shifting baseline that weakens the case for a single past target.
Targets now depend on how degraded the site is, what can realistically be restored, local views and cost.
Some scientists argue that even if the original state cannot return, a 'novel ecosystem' still has valuable functions.
Restoration targets are described as moral and political as well as scientific choices.

contested_note: Opinions differ widely on how to set restoration goals and judge success.
notes: Draws on Ecological restoration § Definition and § Rationale.

definition.text: Ecological succession is the way a community of living things changes over time, especially after a disturbance.

facts.text: Ecosystems often move from a few pioneer species to a complex community of many interdependent species.
Restoration often means starting, helping or speeding up succession, depending on how severe the disturbance was.
After severe damage, such as in cities, restorers may first have to recreate conditions that let succession happen.

title: Restoration ecology and conservation biology
article: Ecological restoration#Contrasting restoration ecology and conservation biology

definition.text: Two related sciences that both value protecting and restoring habitat, but conservation biology studies species populations while restoration ecology works at the community level.

facts.text: Conservation biology often centres on animals; restoration ecology centres on plants, because projects usually start by establishing plant communities.
Restoration ecology puts more weight on soils, fungi and microbes, the base of land ecosystems.
Restoration ecology became a separate field in the late twentieth century.

title: Restoration versus emission cuts
article: Ecological restoration#Restoration as a substitute for steep emission reductions

definition.text: The debate over relying on nature restoration to fight climate change instead of quickly cutting fossil fuel emissions.

facts.text: Climate benefits of restoration are described as dwarfed by ongoing fossil fuel emissions.
One study concluded land restoration matters but cannot make up for delays in cutting fossil fuel emissions, as it is too slow to lower peak temperatures in coming decades.
Avoiding deforestation is better than clearing and replanting, which causes lasting biodiversity loss and soil damage.
Forestry-based carbon offsetting is controversial and is sometimes criticised as carbon colonialism.

contested_note: Sources dispute how much weight restoration should carry against cutting fossil fuel use.
notes: S:f5bb93ad3e96 says 'the former leads to irreversible effects' while the identical sentence on Afforestation/Reforestation (S:1510eab8d723) says 'the latter'; the Ecological restoration wording looks like an error.

definition.text: The divide between restoration ecology research and the people who carry out restoration on the ground.

facts.text: A 2009 survey ranked the gap as the second most cited limit on the growth of restoration science and practice.
Land managers often find research questions not useful, and studies are often small and controlled, unlike real projects.
Tight budgets mean many projects keep few records, limiting evidence-based advice.

title: International Standards for Ecological Restoration
article: Ecological restoration#International Principles & Standards for the Practice of Ecological Restoration

definition.text: Guidance from the Society for Ecological Restoration that sets out principles and standards for planning, doing and monitoring restoration projects.

facts.text: The first edition came out on December 12, 2016, and the second on September 27, 2019.
They recommend performance measures for industries, communities and governments.
They include a technical appendix on sourcing seeds for restoration.

definition.text: Knowledge Indigenous peoples have built up by observing and managing their environment, which shows restoration has been practised for thousands of years.

facts.text: Indigenous peoples shaped vegetation to meet their needs and sometimes increased populations and biodiversity.
Because such knowledge is tied to place, restorers must take care not to appropriate it, and projects involving Indigenous peoples should be led by them.
California Indians used practices such as concentrated forest burning.

definition.text: Forest restoration is action that speeds the return of a forest's structure, ecological workings and biodiversity toward those of a climax forest, the end stage of natural succession.

facts.text: Climax forests are fairly stable ecosystems with the most biomass, structure and species that climate and soil allow without human disturbance.
It is a special kind of reforestation whose main goals are biodiversity recovery and environmental protection, unlike timber plantations.
It can range from protecting leftover vegetation, by preventing fire or keeping out cattle, to planting trees or sowing seeds directly.
Success is measured by more biodiversity, biomass, productivity, soil organic matter and water-holding capacity, plus the return of rare and keystone species.
Economic measures of success include the value of forest products and services such as watershed protection and carbon storage.
Payments for ecological services and forest products can give local people strong reasons to restore forests.
Active restoration can speed carbon recovery in human-modified tropical forests by as much as 50%.
Because climate shapes climax forests, climate change may shift restoration goals.

definition.text: Forest landscape restoration (FLR) is a planned process to regain ecological integrity and improve human well-being across deforested or degraded landscapes.

facts.text: It links restoration at single sites to goals for a whole landscape, agreed through participation among stakeholders.
The concept grew out of work by the IUCN, WWF, the World Resources Institute and the International Tropical Timber Organization.
It seeks compromises between the needs of people and wildlife, with local communities central to planning.
Desired outcomes include tackling root causes of degradation, settling land-use conflicts, agreeing benefit-sharing and providing watershed services.
An FLR program can mix protecting secondary forest, assisted natural regeneration, framework tree planting, timber plantations and agroforestry.
FAO set up the Forest and Landscape Restoration Mechanism in 2014 to help countries meet the Bonn Challenge.

definition.text: The range of money sources, from loans to grants and public spending, used to plan and carry out forest and landscape restoration.

facts.text: Options are either for-profit, such as debt or loans, or not-for-profit, such as grants, fiscal policy or public spending.
FAO says linking smallholders with investors, local ownership and blended finance help restoration reach scale.
Barriers include a lack of large-scale government funding and smallholders' limited resources and skills.

title: Protecting regrowth from browsing animals
article: Forest restoration#Protecting regeneration areas from browsing animals

definition.text: Shielding young, regrowing forest from deer and other browsing animals that can over-graze seedlings.

facts.text: Over-grazed saplings may be damaged beyond recovery, reducing biodiversity.
Deer fencing is used, or where it is too costly, trees that recover structurally are planted instead.

definition.text: Restoring forest after fire, a heavy cause of forest loss in many parts of the world.

facts.text: Fires may be set to clear land for crops, or occur naturally or on purpose in dry areas.
Burnt land can lose much ecosystem value and degrade further through erosion and desertification.
Sometimes fire raises a site's biodiversity, and restoration plans then look for a different land use.

title: Great Green Wall (Africa)

definition.text: The Great Green Wall is an African Union project, adopted in 2007, first meant to stop desertification in the Sahel by planting a belt of trees from Djibouti to Senegal.

facts.text: The wall was planned to be 15 km wide and 7,775 km long.
It grew from tree planting into a mosaic of green, productive landscapes using water harvesting and local land-use methods.
It aims by 2030 to restore 100 million hectares of degraded land, capture 250 million tonnes of carbon dioxide and create 10 million jobs.
A 2020 UNCCD report found only 4% of the planned area covered, with 4 million hectares planted.
In January 2021 partners pledged USD 14.3 billion for the Great Green Wall Accelerator; by March 2023, $2.5 billion had been paid out.
As of 2024, about 30 million hectares had been restored, 30% of the target.
In 2023 it was said to face collapse from terrorism, weak political leadership and too little funding.
Critics point to colonial roots of the term 'desertification' and mostly European funding, seen as neocolonialism.

contested_note: Critics question its progress, funding and colonial framing, and some call for scrapping it.

conflicts.text: The $8-billion project would create 350,000 rural jobs by 2030.
conflicts.note: The lead gives 10 million jobs by 2030 as the goal (S:4032cccb380e).

conflicts.text: The estimated $33 billion to fund the project.
conflicts.note: Another sentence calls it an $8-billion project (S:eec8f102e8b5).

notes: A map of the planned belt across the Sahel would help.

definition.text: Rewetting returns a drained peatland to its original waterlogged state so peat-forming plants can recover.

facts.text: It keeps soil moist and slows drainage by blocking and filling canals; dams of peat or plastic block channels and gullies.
A higher water table slows plant decay and so cuts greenhouse gas emissions.
Wet conditions produce some methane, but because methane stays in the air for a shorter time, the long-run effect is likely cooling.

title: Paludiculture

definition.text: Paludiculture is farming on drained peatlands after they have been rewetted.

facts.text: Raising the water table gets the carbon-storing peatland working again.
The land serves two uses at once: a carbon sink and a farm.
Possible crops include berries, herbs, timber and biomass for biofuel.
Peatlands cover only 3% of land but store more than 450 gigatonnes of carbon, more than all forests.

contested_note: Whether a given peatland farming practice counts as sustainable paludiculture is debated.

definition.text: Estimates of the money value society gains from restoring peatlands, compared with what restoration costs.

facts.text: Restoring 20% of Scotland's peatland was estimated to bring benefits of £80 to £336 million per year.
A later study found restoration by 2027 would give the UK £191 million a year in benefits after restoration costs.
Delaying restoration until 2039–2050 would lose much of these benefits.

title: Rewilding

definition.text: Rewilding is a kind of ecological restoration that aims to raise biodiversity and restore natural processes while reducing human influence.

facts.text: Its key feature is replacing human management with natural processes.
Unlike other restoration, it accepts novel ecosystems with new species and interactions.
It often brings back large mammals to rebuild food webs and make ecosystems self-regulating.
The term was coined by Earth First! in 1990 and given a scientific basis by Michael Soulé and Reed Noss in 1998.
Soulé and Noss built it on 'cores, corridors and carnivores': large protected areas, links between them, and large predators.
It is promoted as a natural climate solution through carbon storage, flood management and lower wildfire risk.
In a Guyana forest, going from 5 to 35 mammal species raised tree and soil carbon four to five times.
The UN lists rewilding as one method needed for large-scale restoration by 2030 under the 30x30 campaign.

contested_note: Rewilding is described as controversial, with critics questioning its evidence and effect on farming and livelihoods.

definition.text: Active rewilding covers rewilding approaches that involve human intervention.

facts.text: It can include reintroducing or moving species, engineering habitat, and removing man-made structures and troublesome introduced species.
Rewilding methods range from land protection and connectivity to removing infrastructure and reintroducing species.

title: Pleistocene rewilding

definition.text: Pleistocene rewilding is bringing back surviving Ice Age megafauna, or close stand-ins for extinct ones, to restore how ecosystems work.

facts.text: Advocates say ecosystems that evolved alongside such animals now lack large mammals and may collapse.
Critics say today's communities cannot be assumed to work like those of 10,000 years ago.

contested_note: Advocates and critics disagree whether modern ecosystems resemble Pleistocene ones enough for this to work.

title: Trophic rewilding

definition.text: Trophic rewilding restores food-web interactions, especially top predators controlling plant-eaters, by (re)introducing species so ecosystems regulate themselves.

facts.text: Apex predators may be needed to stop grazers from over-breeding and stripping vegetation, as in the mass starvation at Oostvaardersplassen in the Netherlands.

contested_note: It is debated whether predators control prey mainly by killing them or indirectly through fear.

definition.text: Ecosystem engineers are living things that clearly reshape the structure of their habitats.

facts.text: Rewilding uses beaver, elephants, bison, elk, and cattle and pigs as stand-ins for extinct aurochs and wild boar.
Large mammals shape the structure and makeup of habitats.

title: Criticism of rewilding

definition.text: Objections to rewilding from governments, farmers, conservationists and others, about livelihoods, evidence and conflicts with people.

facts.text: Some officials say strict no-extraction areas limit people's ability to earn a living; others reply that ecotourism creates jobs.
Some farmers say it abandons productive farmland while world population grows.
Some scientists say its benefits lack evidence and it may pull funding from better-supported conservation.
Reintroduced predators can cause conflict, such as brown bears in Trentino, Italy.

contested_note: Supporters and critics disagree on rewilding's economic and conservation effects.
notes: Article anchor is the parent Criticism section; subsections are Compatibility with economic activity, Farming, Harm to conservation, Human-wildlife conflict.

definition.text: The UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration is a United Nations campaign running from 2021 to 2030 to promote the repair of degraded ecosystems worldwide.

facts.text: It aims to fight climate change, protect biodiversity, and improve food security and water supply through restoration.
It began on World Environment Day, 5 June 2021, after the UN General Assembly adopted it on 1 March 2019, following a proposal by El Salvador.
The UN asked nations to deliver existing restoration pledges of over 1 billion hectares, an area bigger than China.
About half the world's GDP depends directly on nature, yet people use up natural resources about 1.6 times faster than nature restores them.
The UN defines ecosystem restoration as halting and reversing degradation so that ecosystem services improve and biodiversity recovers.
It is co-led by UNEP and the Food and Agriculture Organization.
Recommended approaches include regenerative agriculture, ecological restoration and rewilding.

definition.text: Assisted natural regeneration (ANR), or managed regrowth, is protecting and caring for tree seedlings that sprout naturally so a forest regrows.

facts.text: It removes barriers to regrowth, such as weeds, poor soil, fire-prone grasses like Imperata, and other disturbance.
New trees are planted only where needed, which is called enrichment planting.
It is cheaper than replanting because it skips nurseries, site preparation and raising seedlings.
Forests grow faster than they would on their own, adding to carbon storage.
It needs enough natural seedlings (200 to 800 per hectare suggested), nearby seed sources and control of grazing, fire and logging.
Labour such as weeding and firebreaks can create local jobs.
Regrowing trees from roots that survive in cleared land is also called farmer-managed natural regeneration, and seedlings survive better because roots already reach groundwater.
A practical approach is to plant tough, fast-growing native species that start rebuilding degraded land.

title: Bonn Challenge

definition.text: The Bonn Challenge is a global goal to restore 150 million hectares of degraded and deforested land by 2020 and 350 million hectares by 2030.

facts.text: Germany and the IUCN launched it in Bonn on 2 September 2011.
The IUCN estimates meeting it would bring about $84 billion a year in net benefits, helping rural incomes.
Meeting it is estimated to shrink the carbon dioxide emissions gap by 11-17%.
Reaching 350 million hectares by 2030 could bring up to $9 trillion in net benefits.
Nearly half of the pledges were found to be land set aside for commercial wood use.
Pakistan's Billion Tree Tsunami restored 350,000 hectares, beating its Bonn Challenge pledge.

conflicts.text: Restoring 150 million hectares by 2020 would sequester 1 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide, reducing the current emission gap by 20%.
conflicts.note: Another lead sentence gives an 11-17% reduction of the emissions gap for meeting the challenge (S:8456f083938a); the two may refer to different targets.

notes: Marine coastal ecosystem sentence S:8fb932542293 gives 350 million km2, likely an error for hectares.

title: African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative

definition.text: AFR100, the African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative, aims to bring 100 million hectares of degraded land in Africa under restoration by 2030.

facts.text: It is part of the Bonn Challenge.
28 African countries have committed a total of 113 million hectares.
Latin America's Initiative 20x20 is a similar regional effort aiming to restore 20 million hectares by 2030.

notes: No page of its own; mentioned on Bonn Challenge and UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration.

title: Trillion Tree Campaign

definition.text: The Trillion Tree Campaign is a project to plant one trillion trees worldwide to fight climate change.

facts.text: It grew out of the Billion Tree Campaign, inspired by Wangari Maathai and launched by UNEP in 2006.
In December 2011 UNEP handed the program to the youth-led Plant-for-the-Planet Foundation.
In 2015 Tom Crowther found about 3 trillion trees exist; planting 1.2 trillion more was later estimated to offset 10 years of human CO2 emissions.
By 30 May 2021, 13.96 billion trees had been planted, 1.396% of the goal.

notes: S:9d230b3ba9f9 flagged FAILED VERIFICATION; used only for the launch year and body.

definition.text: An exclosure is a fenced-off patch of grazing land that keeps out cattle, deer or other browsing animals.

facts.text: Most exclosures are set aside for regreening, with no wood cutting or grazing.
In developing countries people earn from them through grass harvesting, beekeeping and other non-timber products.
Nearby communities may earn carbon credits for the CO2 they store, and in Tigray, Ethiopia, the revenue is reinvested in village priorities.

definition.text: Land rehabilitation is returning damaged land, for example after industry or natural disasters, to some degree of its former state.

facts.text: Mining, farming and forestry are among the activities that degrade land.
In parts of the United States, 'reclamation' means returning disturbed land to an improved state.
Mine rehabilitation reshapes waste dumps against erosion, covers them with topsoil and plants vegetation to hold the material.
Sulfide-bearing ore is covered with clay so rain and air cannot turn it into sulfuric acid.
Closed mines can be reused for heat, water or methane recovery, keeping the methane out of the air.

definition.text: A rehabilitation security bond is money a mining company must put up before mining begins to guarantee it will repair the land afterwards.

facts.text: In Australia, rehabilitation is a legal duty backed by bonds, and could create regional jobs and investment if laws were enforced.
Australian mine rehabilitation bonds total $9.49 billion, with NSW's at $2.68bn in 2019.
NSW's Auditor General questioned whether bonds are big enough to cover full rehabilitation costs.
Reclaiming abandoned mines in the US is estimated to cost $9.6bn, paid from operating mines and public sources.

definition.text: Land restoration, which may include rewilding, is returning land to a different or earlier state for a chosen purpose.

facts.text: Purposes include making land safe, stabilising ecological communities, cleaning up pollution, creating novel ecosystems or returning to a historical condition.
It is an antidote to damage caused mostly by people, such as pollution, deforestation, salination and species endangerment.
It differs from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems to make way for farming or building.
It can increase the supply of valuable ecosystem services.
Projects choose a reference ecosystem to measure success against and survey existing conditions first.
Traditional ecological knowledge used alongside Western science is becoming the mainstream approach.

definition.text: Restoring land lost to desertification, done in phases that first fix the soil and then enrich it.

facts.text: First, grasses, shelterbelts, windbreaks and woodlots fix the soil so dunes stop moving.
Shelterbelts are rows of trees set across the prevailing wind.
Next, nitrogen-fixing plants enrich the soil, crops are grown at once, and crops are rotated yearly to avoid draining trace elements.

definition.text: Mine reclamation is reshaping mined land so it again works as an ecosystem or can be used economically.

facts.text: It happens after mining ends, but may be planned before a mine is permitted.
The practice began at the start of the 20th century, and many abandoned mines were never reclaimed.
Full return to the original landscape is often impossible; usually the limit is making mine waste physically and chemically stable.
In open-cut mines, rock backfills the pit, stored soil and topsoil go on top, and vegetation is restored.
Reforestation is the main way of restoring post-mining sites.
Under the US 1977 SMCRA law, operators post a performance bond equal to the reclamation plan's cost, released only after reclamation succeeds.
A coal tax of $0.12 per ton underground and $0.28 per ton surface-mined funds reclamation of abandoned US mines.

definition.text: The Forestry Reclamation Approach (FRA) is a set of guidelines for regrowing forest on land mined for coal.

facts.text: It calls for at least four feet of good rooting material, such as topsoil or weathered sandstone, loosely graded to avoid compaction.
It plants early successional trees for wildlife and soil, then commercially valuable crop trees.

title: Novel ecosystem

definition.text: A novel ecosystem is one that human activity, land use and climate change have pushed into a mix of species and conditions never seen before.

facts.text: They are human-altered places where a self-sustaining ecosystem forms without ongoing human management.
The term was first used in 2006.
Defining features: change past a threshold, caused by people, and self-sustaining afterwards.
Without rapid climate action they could cover more than 50% of Earth's land by 2100 and 80% by 2300.
Examples include a quarry colonised by weedy species and coral reefs taken over by algae.
Some scientists argue that even if an ecosystem cannot return to its original state, a novel ecosystem's functions are still valuable.

contested_note: Researchers disagree on how to define novelty, and some argue against any sharp definition.

verification.title: Towards a novel biosphere in 2300: rapid and extensive global and biome-wide climatic novelty in the Anthropocene
verification.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
verification.evidence: Our analysis shows that unless rapid mitigation measures are taken, the coverage of novel ecosystems could be over 50% of the land surface by 2100 under all change scenarios.

title: Managing novel ecosystems

definition.text: The choices for handling novel ecosystems: tolerating them, managing against them back toward history, or managing for them as new systems.

facts.text: Too little funding and information has made tolerance and inaction the default.
Managing against them means traditional restoration: removing non-native species and bringing back natives toward historical benchmarks.
Fast climate change often makes historical baselines unreachable, so scientists increasingly aim for resilient, adaptive ecosystems.

contested_note: Managing for novel ecosystems is described as more controversial than restoring historical states.

title: Anthromes
article: Novel ecosystem#Ecocentric approach to novel ecosystems

definition.text: Anthromes are the land's biomes in their modern, human-altered form, mapped by patterns of lasting human land use.

facts.text: Each anthrome is a patchwork of land uses, often with areas partly reclaimed by nature.
Groups include intensive land-use biomes such as croplands, pastures, plantations and cities, and artificial wetlands such as reservoirs and rice paddies.

title: Passive rewilding

definition.text: Passive rewilding is letting land, usually after it has been abandoned, return to nature with little or no human management.

facts.text: It is also called natural or spontaneous regeneration, and differs from other rewilding because people do not intervene directly.
Its three parts are letting wildlife return, reconnecting landscapes so plants and animals can move, and allowing disturbances such as fires, pests and floods.
Land is left to rewild either on purpose or because of socio-economic change.
Forests have been regrowing on abandoned pastures and scrub across Europe and North America.
In Spain, regrowth on abandoned farmland has raised fire risk, and effects on biodiversity depend on the site.
The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone has seen boars, lynxes, wolves and brown bears return.
Bruce Sterling coined 'involuntary park' in 1998 for once-inhabited places left to go wild.

notes: Rewilding#Passive rewilding (S:bf9a0fd5d625) covers the same concept; fold if drafted there.

definition.text: A secondary forest is woodland that has grown back largely by natural processes after logging, clearing for farming or a similar natural disturbance.

facts.text: It differs from old-growth (primary) forest, which has not recently been disturbed.
Cleared land is first taken over by pioneer species, then shrubs, and finally trees of the original forest.
It typically takes 40 to 100 years to start to resemble the original old-growth forest.
Most forests of the United States and Europe are secondary forest.
Species numbers can recover quickly, but which species and how common they are take much longer.
Secondary forests store more soil carbon than tree plantations, though less than primary forests.
They protect watersheds, provide habitat, link forest fragments and supply wood to rural communities.
By some estimates, more than 50 acres of new secondary forest grow for every acre of old-growth forest cut.

verification.title: Biodiversity recovery of Neotropical secondary forests
verification.evidence: Secondary forests take a median time of five decades to recover the species richness of old-growth forest (80% recovery after 20 years) based on rarefaction analysis.

verification.title: Soil Carbon Stocks Decrease following Conversion of Secondary Forests to Rubber (Hevea brasiliensis) Plantations
verification.evidence: We found that forest-to-rubber plantation conversion resulted in losses of soil carbon stocks by an average of 37.4±4.7 (SE) Mg C ha(-1) in the entire 1.2-m depth over a time period of 46 years, which was equal to 19.3±2.7% of the initial soil carbon stocks in the secondary forests.

definition.text: Species reintroduction is deliberately releasing a species into the wild, from captivity or from other places, where it can survive.

facts.text: The aim is a healthy, genetically varied, self-sustaining population where the species had died out, or a boost to an existing one.
Candidates are usually threatened or endangered, but reintroduction can also control pests, such as wolves curbing too many deer.
Individuals come either from wild populations (in situ) or from captivity such as zoos or botanic gardens (ex situ); wild sourcing is preferred where possible.
Source populations should resemble the release site genetically and ecologically so the animals or plants are well adapted.
Captive-bred animals can adapt to captivity, becoming tamer, less stress-tolerant and losing local adaptations.
Small reintroduced populations risk inbreeding, which can erode crucial genetic diversity.
There is no agreed definition of success, but it should produce viable, self-sustaining populations long term.

title: Cost-effectiveness of restoration

definition.text: The comparison of what restoring ecosystems costs with the benefits it returns, and with the cost of doing nothing.

facts.text: On average, benefits of ecosystem restoration exceed the initial investment tenfold, while the cost of inaction is at least three times the cost of restoring.
Restoring 350 million hectares by 2030 could generate US$9 trillion in ecosystem services and remove 13 to 26 gigatons of greenhouse gases.
Degradation of land and marine ecosystems costs about 10% of annual global GDP (c. $6.3 trillion).
UK peatland restoration by 2027 was estimated to yield £191 million a year net of restoration costs.
Assisted natural regeneration cuts costs by skipping site preparation and seedling raising, appealing for large projects.
In Oregon, each dollar invested in restoration generated another 1.4 to 2.4 dollars of economic activity.
When clean-up and restoration costs fall late in a project, a high discount rate makes the project look better than it is.

notes: Phrase concept with no page of its own; draws on UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration, Peatland restoration, Assisted natural regeneration, Restoration economy and Net present value.
